title: pool-health-hypotheses-and-hunt-notes
content:
Summary:

This is an investigation scratchpad and action-handoff for recurring pool-level degradations observed in dedicated GPU pools during late-night bursts. The doc bundles an immediate triage checklist, short mitigation playbook, a prioritized hypothesis list (noisy neighbor vs autoscaler misconfig vs infra degradation), and concrete follow-ups for the next sprint. Not final — intended to be an SRE working doc for rotation and the infra/serving teams to iterate on.

Observed symptom pattern (recurring):
- 23:30–02:30 PST high tail latency for small inference requests; median OK but 95/99 spikes.
- Successful token throughput drops while total scheduled GPU utilization reports remain below 70% on affected nodes.
- Concurrently, increased kernel stalls visible in driver logs and elevated PCIe/NVLink error counts on a subset of cards.
- Autoscaler logs show repeated scale-up attempts that are throttled or delayed; some nodes enter Cordon state unexpectedly.

Quick timeline (example incident Dec 6):
- 23:12: first 95th latency alert fired for model-route-prod-12.
- 23:18: oncall ran initial mitigation: set route fallback to smaller model, latency improved briefly.
- 23:25: kube events show scale-up initiated -> 5 new pods scheduled -> NotReady until 23:47.
- 23:48: manual cordon/uncordon of node-7 cause temporary improvement; new spike at 00:05.

High-value signals to capture during hunt (prioritized):
1) Node-level GPU metrics: gpu_utilization, memory_used, ecc_errors, power, temperature.
   - Query example (PromQL-ish, adapt to our metrics): 'avg_over_time(gpu_utilization{pool="dedicated-x"}[15m])' and 'increase(gpu_ecc_errors_total[1h])'.
2) Driver/kernel stalls: dmesg/syslog for 'GPU HANG' or 'nvlink' errors.
3) Pod-level scheduling events: pending->containerCreating delays, image pull backoffs, and GPU plugin events.
4) Autoscaler logic traces: reason for not adding nodes, recent config changes (target_utilization, max_burst, cooldown).
5) Network fabric and storage metrics: packet drops, NVMe latency for model weights, NFS disconnects.
6) Model-level request patterns: sudden microbursts (many short requests) vs long-running batch jobs.

Immediate mitigation playbook (oncall quick-run):
- Step 0: Triage channel: @sre-oncall + infra-oncall + serving-runtime (start thread with incident id INF-xxxx).
- Step 1: Pin traffic off suspect model routes to a standby variant (route-level fallback) to reduce tail load.
- Step 2: If tail latency persists, identify top-3 busiest pods on affected nodes and move them using 'kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data' after scaling replicas down where safe. Mark node as 'quarantined' (label: pool-quarantine=true).
- Step 3: If node-level ECC or nvlink errors present, immediately cordon node and open hardware ticket for replacement; re-schedule workloads away from node.
- Step 4: If autoscaler appears stuck (scale-ups delayed), check autoscaler-controller logs for rate-limit messages and 'scale_down_disabled' flags; if misconfig suspected, revert last autoscaler change (see linked PR).
- Step 5: Restore traffic incrementally and monitor 95/99 latencies for 30 minutes.

Investigation hypotheses (ranked; tests to confirm):
A) Noisy neighbor with kernel-level stalls: heavy long-running workload on same GPU causes kernel scheduling delays affecting small requests.
   - Confirm: correlate per-pod GPU pci bus activity, nvlink errors, and 'dmesg' stalls.
   - Test: isolate the heavy workload to its own dedicated pool or quota; measure tail latency.
B) Autoscaler misconfiguration causing slow scale-up/cooldown interaction with burst traffic.
   - Confirm: inspect autoscaler events, backlog metrics, and timeline of pod readiness vs incoming request rate.
   - Test: temporarily increase max_burst and lower cooldown to see if recovery latency improves (do in canary environment first).
C) Underlying node hardware degradation (thermal/power throttling, firmware): intermittent ECC and PCIe errors.
   - Confirm: hw telemetry, manufacturer sensor logs, cross-compare nodes on same rack.
   - Test: move workloads off node and run a synthetic load test.
D) Scheduler or kube GPU plugin regression after recent runtime upgrade.
   - Confirm: compare kubelet/gpu-plugin versions across nodes; check for recent node pool upgrades in release-engineering history.

Useful commands and probes (copyable from this doc oncall-use):
- Check GPU health quickly: 'kubectl -n kube-system exec -it gpu-health-collector -- /bin/sh -c "nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,UTIL,HEALTH"'
- Pod scheduling trouble: 'kubectl describe pod <pod> --namespace=model-prod' then 'kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<node>'
- Driver/kernel logs: 'journalctl -k -u kubelet -S "2026-01-01" | grep -i nvlink'
- Autoscaler trace: 'kubectl logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system --since=2h | grep -i scale'

Data to capture for postmortem (minimum dataset):
- Prometheus timeseries for 1h before to 1h after incident for: 95th/99th latency, pod_gpu_util, pod_gpu_memory, node_gpu_ecc_errors, pods_pending, cluster_cpu_pressure, autoscaler_decisions.
- Node-level dmesg and nvidia-smi output snapshots.
- Autoscaler event log with timestamps.
- List of recently merged infra PRs (last 72h) and any scheduled node upgrades.

Immediate action items (owners & ETA):
- Ethan Morales: add an automated 'node-quarantine' label and small automation to cordon + notify infra (ETA: 3d).
- Zoe Kim: create a metric dashboard tile that shows 'gpu_ecc_errors' correlated with tail latency (ETA: 2d).
- Malik Thompson: run a controlled noisy-neighbor test in private dev pool to reproduce and capture kernel logs (ETA: 1 week).
- Priya: review autoscaler config flags (target_utilization, burst_ratio, cooldowns) and propose a safe canary change for staged environments (ETA: 4d).

Longer-term mitigations (candidates for next quarter):
- Per-pool protected lanes: enforce strict placement classes so long-running batch inference cannot colocate with latency-sensitive workloads.
- Autoscaler policy enforcement: introduce an integration test where simulated microbursts verify scale-up latency within SLO before merging autoscaler changes.
- Hardware telemetry escalation path: wire ECC/PCIe anomaly alerts to an oncall infra page and auto-open hardware tickets when thresholds exceed X.
- Scheduler QoS isolation: investigate using node taints/tolerations for high-variance workloads.

Open questions and unknowns:
- Are there correlated storage/NVMe spikes that coincide with the GPU stalls? We need a storage team sync.
- Does a model rollout or cache warm-up pattern precede the bursts? Product/serving team to confirm.

Notes to handoff to postmortem owner:
- Collect the dataset above and run a cross-correlation analysis between 'nvlink/ecc' and 'inference tail latency' using at least 10 incidents.
- If hardware signals are present on >2 nodes in same rack, open priority hardware replacement and flag for potential fleet-wide firmware sweep.

Appendix: quick links and references
- Autoscaler config PR: https://github.com/repo/infra/pull/512 (related to burst_ratio change)
- Recent hardware incident ticket: HWT-2025-09 (for reference on ECC handling)
- Confluence: pool-capacity-guidelines

End of scratchpad — keep iterating. If you add findings, append with date and name so we can track changes across rotations.
